en: The Chapter on Lodgings (*śayanāsanavastu*):
Summary Verse (*uddāna*).
The Śākyas, the five groups, and the ten; communal property and individual property, by way of the destruction of property.
One should cause the spreading out [of robes] to be done; the ground and the forest are for the three robes.
The forest is to be cleared away; the elder monk becomes the last of the group of six regarding gains.
Veneration is due to elder monks.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now at that time, while a great many monks were seated together and assembled in the assembly hall, this kind of conversation arose among them:
"Venerable ones, who among us is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped?
To whom should we perform acts of salutation, prostration, rising from our seats, joining our palms, and respectful conduct?
Who among us deserves to enjoy the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food?"
In that regard, some say, "It is a Śākyan who has gone forth";
others say, "It is a Brāhmaṇa who has gone forth"; and still others say, "It is a Kṣatriya who has gone forth."
Others were Vaiśyas who had gone forth; others were Śūdras who had gone forth;
others had gone forth from high families, not from low ones.
He has gone forth from a wealthy family that is not destitute;

he is preeminent, handsome, pleasing to behold, and inspiring; he is endowed with excellent speech and a beautiful voice; he is renowned, possessed of great merit, a master of the Sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the Mātṛkās; he is learned, a preacher of the Dharma, an elder, and a nobleman. He is a forest-dweller, one who wears the three robes, one who wears felt garments, one who wears rag-robes from dust-heaps, one who lives on alms-food, one who eats at a single sitting, one who refuses food after rising from his seat, one who dwells at the foot of a tree, one who dwells in cemeteries, and one who dwells in the open air.

"The one who lives by gleaning, the one who uses whatever mat is provided, the one who has attained the perception of impermanence—as described previously—up to the Arhat who dwells in the eight liberations.
Others said, "Venerable sirs, we do not agree with all of us regarding these various designations.
Let us go to where the Blessed One is."
"Having approached, we shall ask the Blessed One about this matter;
we will retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to us.
Then, a great number of monks went to where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the many monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, while we many monks were sitting together and assembled in the assembly hall, this kind of conversation arose among us."
"As before, up until: 'We shall retain it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to us.
Therefore, Venerable Sir, we ask the Blessed One this very matter: whom among us should one honor, revere, respect, and worship?"
As before, up to the point of consuming the foremost alms-food;
the Blessed One said:
"O monks, you must honor, revere, respect, and worship the most senior among you."
"One should perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising from one's seat, joining the palms, and respectful conduct;
and he is worthy of receiving from you the foremost seat, the foremost water, and the foremost alms-food.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"A monk who is more senior must be honored by you;
as before, up to [the point of] enjoying the seat of honor.
O elder householders!
...and so forth,
are not worthy of veneration; O monks, they show honor, respect, esteem, and worship toward lay householders who are elders.
Having heard this, the brahmins and householders reproached, reviled, and censured [him], saying:
"We are noble ones who enjoy sensual pleasures and are sunk in the mire of desire;
how can you show us such honor?"
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I spoke with reference to those who have gone forth, not to householders."
"Monks, seeing the elders of other sects, they show them respect, honor, esteem, and worship.
The Blessed One said:
"In this case, I spoke with reference to those who follow the Dharma, and not to outsiders."
Seeing those novice monks who had gone forth when they were old, people honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped them;
the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I spoke with reference to those who are fully ordained, not to novice monks."
Those who had recently received full ordination showed respect, reverence, honor, and veneration toward the elders.
The Blessed One said:
"One should pay homage after asking each other about the number of years since one's ordination."
When they were asked, they spoke of their years since birth;
the Blessed One said:
"One should ask about the number of years since full ordination."
The monks did not know [how many years of seniority they had];
the Blessed One said:
The *sāmayika* [observances] should be announced;
the monks did not know how many *sāmayikas* there were,
so the Blessed One said:
Monks, there are these five periods: the winter period, the summer period, the rainy period, the short rainy period, and the long rainy period;
among these, the winter period consists of four months.
The summer season consists of four months;
the rainy season consists of one month;
the post-rainy season consists of one day and night.
The long rainy season consists of three months less one night;
having thus announced the seasonal period, he who was previously ordained is to be saluted.
Furthermore, four other types of monks are also to be saluted.
Who are the four to be honored? First, for the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, and for the generation including recluses and brahmins—
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is to be venerated by all, including gods and humans; all those who have gone forth are to be venerated by householders;
and among all those who are ordained, those ordained earlier are to be venerated by those ordained later—with the exception of a bhikṣuṇī.
Even for her who has been fully ordained for a hundred years, a monk who has been ordained on that very day is to be venerated;
one who is fully ordained is to be venerated by everyone who is not fully ordained.
There are ten who are not to be venerated:

Which ten? One who is on probation (*pārivāsika*), one who is on fundamental probation (*mūlapārivāsika*), one whose probation has been completed (*paryuṣitaparivāsa*), one undergoing the period of reconciliation (*mānāpyacārika*), one who has completed the period of reconciliation (*caritamānāpya*), one suspended for not seeing [the offense], one suspended for not making amends,
one suspended for not relinquishing an evil view, and every householder.
And everyone who was not fully ordained [was excluded].
When the Blessed One had prescribed the *yathāvṛddhikā* (the order according to seniority), the monks then honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped one another.
Honoring, respecting, revering, and worshipping one another, they flourish in wholesome qualities like a lotus in water.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, when the Blessed One had prescribed [the rules] according to seniority, then the monks honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped one another;
honoring, revering, esteeming, and worshipping one another, they increased in wholesome qualities like a lotus in water."
The Blessed One said:

"O monks, what is the wonder here that now, by me—who am free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and fully liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair;

who am omniscient, possessed of all-encompassing knowledge, and have attained mastery over all knowledge and its objects—having established the protocol of seniority and relying upon that protocol of seniority, the monks honor and revere one another?"
As before, up to: "or like a blue lotus in the water.

Now, listen to how—by me, while still possessed of passion, hatred, and delusion, not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair, and with a body fallen into ruin—having established the *yathāvṛddhikā* (the assembly according to seniority), and having relied upon that *yathāvṛddhikā*, the entire population of Jambudvīpa was for the most part reborn in the sublime realm of the Trāyastriṃśa gods. Listen to that.
The Story of the Francolin Partridge, the Hare, the Monkey, and the Elephant
Once upon a time, monks, in a certain dense forest in the kingdom of Kāśī, four creatures lived together: a partridge, a hare, a monkey, and an elephant.
They dwelt with one another in friendship, united, harmonious, and in mutual delight; free from dispute and without fear, they passed their time living as they pleased.
Then, at a later time, a thought arose among them:
"Friends, we are established in mutual friendship, living together, united, in harmony, and without dispute;
yet we do not know whom among us we should honor, revere, respect, and worship.
What if we were to establish a protocol according to seniority?"
They began to converse with one another, saying,
"Who among us is the eldest?
Thereupon, Kapiñjala pointed out a banyan tree.
"Sirs, by whom and of what size was this banyan tree seen? The elephant replied, "As I was traveling along this path with my herd, it was seen by me; it is equal to my own height in stature."
The monkey said:
"While traveling along this path with my troop, I saw this [tree]; it is exactly equal to me in height.
They replied:
"You are older than he," [the hare said].
The hare replied,
"Even I have licked the drops of dew from the leaves of this two-leaved plant with my tongue."
They said,
"You too are old among these two.
Kapiñjala replied:
"Behold this banyan tree, which has assumed a massive form.
They replied, "We see it. [He said,] "Having eaten its fruits, I voided my excrement in this spot, and from that this tree was born."
They said:
"If that is so, you are the eldest among us all.
Thereupon, the elephant began to show honor to everyone.
The monkey [approached] the hare and the francolin; the hare [approached] the francolin alone;
thus, honoring one another according to their seniority, they wandered here and there within that forest thicket.
When uneven and low-lying regions were to be traversed, then the monkey would mount the elephant, the hare the monkey, and the quail the hare.
As their affection thus increased and they became full of mutual respect, this thought arose in them:
"Sirs, we have grown in affection and are full of respect for one another."
"Let us at least live having undertaken some other wholesome practice;
what shall we do?
Kapinjala said:
"We shall abstain from taking life.
"What kind of taking of life is ours?
Kapinjala replied:

"There are grasses, flowers, and fruits that contain living beings, and there are those that are free of living beings; therefore, from this day forward, we must abandon those with living beings and consume only those free of living beings.
Having abandoned those with living beings, they began to consume those free of living beings.
This occurred to them:
"We have abstained from taking life, but we do not abstain from taking what is not given;
what, then, is our form of taking what is not given?"
Kapiñjala said:
"There are grasses, leaves, flowers, and fruits that have owners, and there are those that have no owners;
therefore, from this day forward, we should abandon those with owners and consume only those that are ownerless."
Having abandoned those things that involve possession, they began to consume those that are free from possession.
This occurred to them:
"We have abstained from taking what is not given, but we have not [abstained] from sexual misconduct."
"What if we were to abstain from sexual misconduct? What kind of sexual misconduct applies to us?
Kapiñjala said:
"We approach those who are approachable, and we also approach those who are unapproachable;
therefore, from this day forward, we shall approach only those who are approachable and not those who are unapproachable."
They went with those who were approachable and not with those who were unapproachable.
This occurred to them: "We are indeed abstaining from sexual misconduct."
But not from false speech;
let us now abstain from false speech.
What kind of false speech is ours?
Kapiñjala said:
"Whatever we may have prattled until now, from this day forward we must not prattle at random anymore."
Speech should be uttered only after having reflected again and again at the proper time;
they do not prattle whatever comes to mind, but rather utter speech only after reflecting again and again at the proper time.
This thought occurred to them:
"We have abstained from false speech,
but we have not yet abstained from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence."
"What if we were to abstain from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants?
Of what nature is this occasion of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants for us?
Kapiñjala replied:
"There are intoxicating fruits and there are non-intoxicating fruits;
therefore, from this day forward, we must abandon the intoxicating fruits and consume only the non-intoxicating fruits.
Having thus abandoned the intoxicating fruits, they began to consume the non-intoxicating fruits.
When they had been established in the five bases of the vow, Kapiṃjala said:
"Sirs, we are now established in the five bases of the vow;
what if we were to establish others as well in the five bases of the vow?"
They said,
"We shall do so;
who will establish you?"
The monkey said,
"I shall establish all the monkeys.
Then the hare said:
"I establish all the rabbits, the hairy ones, and the deer," he said;
the elephant replied,
"I establish all the elephants, lions, tigers, and leopards."
Kapiñjala said:
"If it be so, then in brief, those of you who are without discipline—whether two-footed, four-footed, or winged—I shall establish them all in the five bases of the vows.
Thereupon, all the living beings within the realm of Kāśī, down to those belonging to the animal kingdom, were established in the five bases of the vows.
Not harming one another, they dwell with clear comprehension in that forest grove, living as they please;
through their power, the rain-god has become one who rains at the proper time,
and the trees are always in flower and fruit.
The earth was rich with crops;
those humans were seen living without harming one another,
and the trees always bore flowers and fruit.
The earth was rich with crops;
the king said:
"I govern the kingdom according to the Dharma; this is my power."
The women of the inner apartments, the princes, the ministers, the army commanders, and the merchants and country folk said,
"This is our own power."
The king reflected:
"All of these say, 'It is my power, it is my power';
therefore, it is not known whose power it actually is."
Filled with curiosity, he summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them;
they too did not know.
Eventually, there was a park not far from Vārāṇasī.
There dwelt a seer endowed with the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*), who was honored, revered, and saluted by the entire body of people residing in Vārāṇasī.
Then the king approached that seer, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Great Seer, within my realm, even down to the creatures of the animal realm, they all dwell in mutual non-harm, moving with full awareness and living as they please."
The god sends rain at the proper time, the trees are always laden with flowers and fruit, and the earth is rich with crops.
Therefore, this thought occurred to me:
"I am ruling the kingdom according to the Dharma;
this is my power."
The women of the inner apartments, the princes, the ministers, the army commanders, and the merchants and countryfolk reflected:
"This is our power";
yet it was not known whose power this truly was.
I have a great curiosity; you ought to dispel my doubt:
whose power is this?
He said:
"Great King, this is not through your power, nor that of the harem, nor of the princes, nor of the ministers, nor of the army of soldiers, nor of the merchants and country folk;
rather, there dwell in your realm four living beings."
"This is their power," [he thought];
the king said,
"I shall go and see them."
The seer said:
"Great King, what is the use of those things being seen? Rather, you should adopt and practice that which they have adopted and are practicing.
[The king asked: "What is it that they have adopted and are practicing?"
There are five bases of the vows;
Great Seer, what are those five bases of the vows?
Great King, they do not deprive living beings of life.
They do not steal the property of others; they do not engage in sexual misconduct with those who should not be approached; they do not speak falsehoods.
And they do not practice the drinking of intoxicants;
the king said:
"Great Seer, if that is so, may I too undertake and abide by these five precepts."
Then that king, having undertaken the five precepts, began to live according to them;
because the king lived having undertaken the five precepts, the queens also began to live having undertaken the five precepts;
the princes, the ministers, the army officers, and the people of the towns and countryside also began to live having undertaken the five precepts.
The neighboring frontier kings heard that King Brahmadatta was living having undertaken the five precepts together with his harem, princes, ministers, military officers,

and the people of the towns and countryside; and having heard this, they too began to live having undertaken the five precepts together with their harems, princes, ministers, military officers, and the people of the towns and countryside.
Thus, for the most part, the entire body of people began to live having undertaken the five precepts.
At that time, whoever in Jambudvīpa passed away was reborn, upon the dissolution of the body, among the sublime gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing the assembly of deities being filled, spoke again in verse:
"With reverence and deference, they dwell in the forest of asceticism;
the holy life of Kapiñjala has been proclaimed throughout the world. Thus he said.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who was that kapiñjala at that time, on that occasion, was none other than myself;
the hare was the monk Śāriputra, the monkey was the monk Maudgalyāyana, and the elephant was Ānanda."

Even then, when I had established the practice of seniority (*yathāvṛddhikā*), and by relying on that practice of seniority, the entire population dwelling in Jambudvīpa was for the most part reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
and now too, as I have established the practice of seniority, and by relying on that practice of seniority, the monks— honoring, respecting, revering, and worshipping one another—
increase in wholesome qualities (*kuśalair dharmair*) like a blue lotus in water.

The Buddha praises the order according to seniority: "Therefore, monks, you should dwell with reverence, with deference, and with a sense of awe toward your fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether they be seniors, those of middle standing, or juniors. And why is that?"

Monks, it is impossible that a monk who dwells without respect, without deference, and without being subject to fear toward elders, those of middle standing, and juniors, will fulfill the rules of proper conduct;
it is impossible that he will fulfill the rules of training without first fulfilling the rules of proper conduct.

It is impossible that one will fulfill the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation without first fulfilling the qualities of a trainee (*śaikṣadharma*);
it is impossible that one will attain final nirvana through non-clinging without having fulfilled the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"Monks, it is possible that a monk who dwells with reverence, with deference, and under the influence of fear toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life— whether they be elders, those of middle standing, or those newly ordained— will, after fulfilling the rules of proper conduct (*āsamudācārika-dharma*), fulfill the qualities of one in training (*śaikṣa-dharma*). It is possible that, having fulfilled the qualities of one in training, he will fulfill the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*)."
It is possible that he will fulfill the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation and, through non-clinging, attain final nirvana; this possibility exists.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
That we shall dwell with reverence, with deference, and under the influence of fear toward our fellow celibates— whether they be seniors, those of middle standing, or juniors;
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
Regarding the establishment of monasteries (*vihāra*):
when the five [monks] had been disciplined by the Blessed One, they dwelt in the forest.
They dwell in the forest and become prey for lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas.
The Blessed One reflected:
"Where did the disciples of the former Perfectly Enlightened Ones establish their dwellings?
He saw that it was in the monastery; the Blessed One had also informed him of this by means of the deities.
At that time, there lived in Vārāṇasī a householder named Kalyāṇabhadra.
As his continuum of roots of merit was awakened, this thought occurred to him:
"O, would that I might cause a monastery to be built for the disciples of the Blessed One!"
Rising early in the morning, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached and bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, he sat down to one side.
As the householder Kalyāṇabhadrika sat there to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dharma in many ways, [the Blessed One] remained silent.
Then the householder Kalyāṇabhadrika rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
"If the Blessed One would permit it, I would have a monastery built for the Blessed One’s disciples."
The Blessed One said, "Therefore, householder, I permit you; have it built.
He did not know what kind it was to be made.
The Blessed One said:
"If you have three dwellings constructed, a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) should be built in the center, with two dwellings on either side;
likewise, in a three-winged structure, there should be nine dwellings."
In the center of the four-winged building, facing the gateway-chamber, was the Perfumed Chamber;
on both sides of the gateway-chamber were two cells;
he did not know how many stories should be constructed.
The Blessed One said:
"Monasteries for the monks should be built with five stories; the perfumed chamber (gandhakuṭī) with seven stories;
and the upper pavilion (bālāgrapotikā) with seven stories."
For the nuns, however, monasteries with three stories should be built;
the perfumed chamber (gandhakuṭi) should have five stories; and the upper pavilion (bālāgrapotikā) should have five stories.
The Story of Anāthapiṇḍada: His Birth and Wonders.

At that time, there lived in Śrāvastī a householder named Datta, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging property; he had accumulated wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa itself.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
As he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, in the course of time his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth;
a boy was born.
For him, after performing the extensive birth ceremonies for twenty-one days—three times seven days—the naming was established.
"What shall be the name of the boy?
the kinsmen asked; they replied, "This boy is the son of the householder Datta; therefore, let the boy's name be Sudatta."
The name Sudatta was established for him;
the boy Sudatta was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders...
By two nurses who provided milk;
by two nurses who cleaned him;
and by two nurses who played with him.

He was raised by eight nurses; he grew on milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other various highly refined nourishing foods, and he grew quickly like a lotus in a lake. At a later time, adorned with all ornaments and seated upon his nurse’s hip, he went outside.
A beggar requested an ornament, saying:
"O Prince, I am in need of an ornament;
give me an ornament."
With a joyful mind, he gave that ornament;
having entered his house,
his father questioned the nursemaid about it.
"Where is the prince's ornament?
She replied,
"It was given by the prince to a beggar."
He was adorned with another ornament;
that too was given;
once again he was adorned.
He too was given by him;
that householder addressed his wife:
"My dear, a beautiful son has been born to us."
"He is always delighted by giving.
She said, "Noble son, if that is so, I shall not adorn him any further. He said:
"Lady, we possess immeasurable gold and jewels;
however, there are no craftsmen to fashion ornaments.
Therefore, by all means, he must not be allowed to go outside."
He was being pampered right there inside;
then, on another occasion, when the householder Datta set out for the Ajīravatī River to bathe accompanied by his servants,
the boy Sudatta said:
"Father, I too shall go," he said; but the father began to deceive him, saying:
"Son, there is excellent water right here."
"The river is infested with crocodiles;
this nurse will bathe you.
He began to weep.
His mother asked,
"Noble son, for what reason is this boy crying?
He related to her exactly what had occurred.
She said:
"Noble son, let her go with you;
what contradiction is there in this?"
"Thinking, 'He will be even more thoroughly protected,' he took him and went to a river;
having bathed him, he established him in a noble family, who then said:"
"Father, for what reason is my protection being provided?
"Son, you have a fault; how so? You give away the ornaments you were given to beggars."
"Father, are you in need of wealth? "Son, who is not in need?
"Father, if that is so, then take me down."
He was brought down by him;
then, having immersed both his hands in the river, he said: "Whatever wealth you have acquired with gold, perform your financial needs with it, and let whatever remains be submerged right here.
Son, do you see treasures hidden within the water?"
"Father, not only those in the water, but even those on land—whether they have owners or are ownerless, whether they are far away or nearby [are given].
The householder Datta, his eyes wide with wonder, reflected:
"It is truly possible for such a master of giving to bestow gifts. Having understood this, he said:
"Son, if it is so, give gifts as you wish";
for this is the natural law: that a son does not become the owner of his father's property as long as his father lives.
Then, at another time, the householder Datta passed away;
Sudatta became the master of the household.
It was reported everywhere that he was constantly providing alms-food to those who were destitute.
The son of the householder Datta became the master of the household, Suddata;
because he bestowed alms-food upon those who were destitute,
he became known by the name Anāthapiṇḍada, the Householder Who Provides for the Destitute.
Then he took a wife from a family of equal status;
he played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her,
and as he was playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him.
In this way, seven sons were born;
he provided for six of them with marriages,
while the seventh was named Sujāta.
He searched for a family of equal status but did not find one;
placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought.
He had a young friend named Madhuskandha;
seeing him thus absorbed in thought,
the latter said:
“Householder, why do you stand there lost in thought with your cheek resting on your hand?
He replied,
“I have provided dowries for my six sons.”

"I am considering which family would be suitable for Sujāta, the seventh son, so that I may arrange his marriage from such a family. He replied, "Remain free from anxiety; I shall search for a family worthy of him."
"In which region?
He replied,
"I am going to the Magadha territory for now."
"Do so. He went to Rājagṛha.
In Rājagṛha there was a certain householder, wealthy, of great means and great possessions, who was the counterpart of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having entered his house and stood in the gateway hall, he said, "May there be well-being! May there be well-being! To which the members of his household replied:
"Brāhmaṇa, what do you seek? A request for a maiden; for whose sake?"
In Śrāvastī there was the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; his son was named Sujāta.
They said, "He is equal to us in family lineage;
however, our bride-price is very great."
"How much is sufficient?
"A hundred horses, a hundred gold coins, a hundred mule-carts, and a hundred maidens from Kamboja.
Thus, Madhuskandha Mānava sent a letter to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada regarding this matter.
He too, having made him recite, said, "Accept it all; I shall give it.
By means of that day and its auspicious moment, he accepted it.
Then, having been fully satisfied with abundant, pure, and excellent food, the young man went to his hall and, having retired to his lodging, became afflicted with cholera.
The brahmins were strangers;
out of fear of impurity, they cast him outside and abandoned him.
By chance, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived at that place.
He was seen by them;
then, having scraped him with a bamboo splinter and rubbed him with pale clay, they bathed him,
taught him the Dharma, and departed.
His dysentery did not subside;
having developed a serene mind toward those two,
he passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
Having gone into the presence of the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, he requested a palace;
he replied:
"Go, for that very Śivikā-gate is your palace."
Having gone there, he became a permanent resident.
The King of Videha sent a hundred Himalayan elephants to King Bimbisāra;
that king then sent a message to Prasenajit, the King of Kosala:
"The King of Videha has sent me a hundred Himalayan elephants;
if you have need of them, send for them.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached King Prasenajit of Kosala.
Having approached King Prasenajit of Kosala, he said this to him:
"Your Majesty, I have some business in Rājagṛha;
having gone there, I shall return."
The king said:
"Excellent! Go, and bring me also a hundred elephants from that place; you shall bring them.
He replied:
"O King, if there is no need for me there, I shall take [the horse];
having come here, I will win over Your Majesty's heart."
The king said: "Excellent; let it be so.
[Then] Anāthapiṇḍada met the Buddha.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, taking a large dowry, went to Rājagṛha.
He stayed in the house of a certain householder, who, rising early in the morning, addressed his household:
"Arise, noble ones! Arise!"
"O gentle-faced ones, split the wood; kindle the sacrificial fire;
cook the rice;
cook the soup."
"Prepare the delicacies;
attend to the arrangements for the circular pavilion.
Then, this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Could it be that this householder is about to hold a wedding or a marriage ceremony?
Or has he invited the entire kingdom for this meal? Or perhaps a guild, a corporation, or an assembly?"

"Having learned that the Magadhan king Śreṇya Bimbisāra has been invited by you for a meal, [the Blessed One asks: 'Householder, have you invited the kingdom for a meal, or the guild, or the corporation, or the assembly, or the Magadhan king Śreṇya Bimbisāra for a meal? [The householder replied:
'No, nor have I invited the kingdom for a meal.'"
"Neither a guild, nor a corporation, nor an assembly, nor even Śreṇya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha, has ever been invited for a meal.
Upon hearing this sound—the word "Buddha"—which the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had never heard before, all his pores bristled with joy. With his hair standing on end, he said this to that householder:
"Householder, who is this so-called Buddha?

Householder, there is a śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, has gone forth from the home to the homeless state out of perfect faith; he is from the Śākya clan."
He has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
he, O householder, is what is called a Buddha.
And who, O householder, is what is called the Saṅgha?

"Householder, there are sons of good family who, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes, have out of perfect faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life, following that very Blessed One who has already gone forth;

[likewise] sons of good family from brahmin families, from vaiśya families, and even from śūdra families, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned saffron robes, have out of perfect faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life."
Having followed that very Blessed One who had gone forth, they too went forth;
this, householder, is what is called the Saṅgha. (Tomorrow...)
"I have invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal at my home;
Householder, where does the Blessed One reside at present?
"In this very city of Rājagṛha, in the Śītavana cemetery."
"Householder, is it possible for us to see that Blessed One? In that case, householder, wait a moment; it is possible that you will see him here tomorrow once he has arrived."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having fallen asleep that night with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha,
approached the Śivaka Gate at the hour he perceived to be dawn, though it was not yet dawn;
for at that time, the Śivaka Gate remained open during two watches of the night.
"Let there not be an obstacle for the messengers coming from the east and those going to the west";
he then saw that the gate of Śivaka was wide open and filled with light.
This thought occurred to him:
"Surely the night has turned to dawn;
for indeed, the gate of Śivaka stands wide open."
Having understood this, he went out from the city by that very light;
and as soon as he had gone out, that light vanished and darkness appeared.
Fear arose within her.
He was struck with trepidation;
his hair stood on end, thinking:
"Lest some human or non-human, or a rogue, should cause me harm, or lest the abundant bride-price remain unpaid."
Having understood this and desiring to turn back, he circumambulated and paid homage to the sacrificial ground of the divine son Madhuskandha;
then, this thought occurred to the divine son Madhuskandha:
"Anāthapiṇḍada the householder must attain the vision of the Truth this very day;
this very day he will abandon the Buddha, the Blessed One, and pay homage to another deity.
Having understood this, [the Blessed One], illuminating the area between Śivaka Gate and the Śītavana cemetery with a sublime radiance, spoke thus to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
Advance, householder;
do not retreat. It will be better for you to advance.
He does not turn back;
for what reason?
A hundred horses, a hundred gold coins, and a hundred mule-drawn chariots.
A hundred chariots drawn by mares, filled with various kinds of wealth, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a single step taken on foot toward a worthy recipient.
Come forward, householder; do not retreat.
For you, it is better to advance.
He does not turn back;
for what reason?
Because there are a hundred Himalayan elephants, adorned with gold and jewels.
Elephants with tusks like plowshafts, massive in body and well-trained,
are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single step taken by him.
Come forward, householder;
do not turn back. For you, it is better to come forward.
He does not turn back;
for what reason? Because there are a hundred Kāmbojan maidens adorned with jeweled earrings.
Wearing golden armlets, with gold coins upon their necks and well-adorned,
they are not worth even a sixteenth part of a single step taken by him.
Come forward, householder;
do not turn back. For you, it is better to come forward.
He did not turn back;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to that son of the gods: "Who are you, good sir?"
"Householder, I am a young brahmin named Madhuskandha,
your own old friend from before.
Having developed a serene mind toward the monks Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, I passed away and was reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."
He is a resident right here at this gateway of Śivikā;
therefore, I say to you: "Go forward, householder, do not turn back."
"It is better for you to advance, not to retreat";
then this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"The Buddha will not be inferior, nor will his proclamation of the Dharma be inferior,
since even the deities now exert themselves with longing to behold that Blessed One."
Having understood this, he went toward the Śītavana cemetery.
At that time, the Blessed One was walking back and forth on a walkway in the open air outside the monastery,
for the most part waiting for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the Blessed One from afar;
having seen him, he approached the Blessed One,
and upon approaching, the householder greeted the Blessed One with a friendly salutation.
"Is the Blessed One sleeping in comfort?
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"In every way, indeed, the brahmin who has attained final nirvana sleeps in comfort."
For he who is liberated and free from acquisitions is not defiled by desires.
Having understood everything here and having subdued attachment and the fever of the heart,
one who is tranquil sleeps happily with a mind that has attained peace.
Then the Blessed One, taking the householder Anāthapiṇḍada with him, entered the monastery and sat down on the prepared seat.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
To the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, who was seated to one side, the Blessed One showed the Dharma through a discourse, exhorted him, inspired him, and gladdened him.
He gladdens them;

he gives a detailed exposition of that Dharma discourse which is to be delivered by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, at the appropriate time— namely, a discourse on generosity, a discourse on ethical conduct, a discourse on heaven, and a discourse on the gratification, the danger, and the corruption of sensual pleasures, as well as the benefits of renunciation, seclusion, and the factors conducive to purification.
He elucidated it;

and when the Blessed One saw that his mind was joyful, pliable, glad, free from hindrances, capable, and competent to understand the preeminent teaching of the Dharma, he then, in detail, elucidated that preeminent teaching of the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—namely, the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Then, while seated on that very seat, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada realized the four noble truths— namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation,
and the path— just as a clean cloth, free from stains and ready for dyeing, takes the dye perfectly when placed in the dye-pot.
In the very same way, while seated on that very seat, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada realized the four noble truths— namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma, crossed beyond doubt, crossed beyond uncertainty, became independent of others, and was no longer led by others, [attained confidence] in the Teacher.

Having attained confidence regarding the teachings and the dharmas, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have truly transcended."
I go for refuge to the Blessed One,
and to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
Please accept me as a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, as one who has gone for refuge with deep faith.
Then the Blessed One said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, what is your name?
"Venerable sir, my name is Sudatta."
"However, I provide alms-food to those who are without protectors;
therefore, people know me as 'the householder Anāthapiṇḍada,' 'the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. From what region do you come, householder?"
"Venerable sir, there is a town of the Kosalans named Śrāvastī in the eastern provinces;
there I dwell.
[Thus Anāthapiṇḍada invited the Buddha to Śrāvastī.]
"May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One for as long as life lasts, together with the community of monks, providing robes, alms-food, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Householder, are there monasteries in Śrāvastī?"
"No, Venerable Sir;
wherever there are monasteries, O householder, there monks consider it proper to come, to go, and to dwell.
May the Blessed One come."
"I shall act in such a way that there will be monasteries in Śrāvastī,
and that the monks will consider it their duty to come, to go, and to dwell there.
The Blessed One consented to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada by remaining silent.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from his presence.
Then, having performed and completed all that was to be done or required in Rājagṛha, he approached the Blessed One once more;
having approached, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, grant me a monk as an assistant, with whom as an assistant I may have a monastery built in Śrāvastī for the sake of the Blessed One. [The Blessed One asked: "Is the populace residing in Śrāvastī obedient?"
He saw the monk Śāriputra;
thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "Pay attention, Śāriputra, to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada together with his retinue, and to the body of people residing in Śrāvastī."
The Venerable Śāriputra consented to the Blessed One by remaining silent;
then the Venerable Śāriputra, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Śāriputra departs for Śrāvastī.
Then, when that very night had passed, the Venerable Śāriputra dressed in the forenoon,
took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagṛha for alms.
Having walked for alms in Rājagṛha and finished his meal, he returned from his alms-round after the meal, and having put away his bedding and seat exactly as he had used them, [he sat down].
Having taken up his bowl and robe, he set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī;
meanwhile, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having taken a great amount of provisions for the road, arrived at Śrāvastī, staying overnight at each successive stage.
As he was entering Śrāvastī, walking from grove to grove, from park to park, from garden to garden, and pacing back and forth, he spoke thus as he wandered about:

"Which will be that spot of earth not too far from and not too near to Śrāvastī, where it is not crowded by day nor noisy at night, having little sound and little clamor, and where there is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and crawling reptiles, so that I may have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One?"

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw Prince Jeta’s park, which was neither too far from nor too near Śrāvastī; it was little-frequented by day, with few distractions, and at night it had little noise, little clamor,
and little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles.
And having seen this, it occurred to him:
"In this place I shall have a monastery built for the Blessed One. As soon as he had entered his own residence, he approached Prince Jeta; having approached, he said this to Prince Jeta:
"O Prince, grant me the grove;
I shall have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One.
He replied:
"Householder, that is not my park;
rather, it is my garden.
For a second and even a third time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to Prince Jeta:
"O Prince, grant me the park;
I shall have a monastery built there for the sake of the Blessed One. [The prince replied:
"It has not been relinquished."
"Householder, my park [is not for sale] even for a covering of ten million pieces of gold.
Then again, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the youth Jeta:
"You have paid the price for the grove, O Prince;
accept this gold and bullion;
the grove is mine."
"Who has received the guest-offering?
You have received the guest-offering.
Thus they fell into a dispute, saying, "I have received it," and "You have not received it."
They set out toward where the officials were;
meanwhile, it occurred to the four world-protectors:
"This householder Anāthapiṇḍada is intent on having a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One."
"Assistance must be rendered to him.
Thereupon, having manifested themselves as judicial officers, they sat down in the court of justice;
the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and Prince Jeta approached the presence of the judicial officers.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika explained this matter in detail to the officials;
they said,
"Young man, you have committed a crime against the park."
"Accept this gold;
the park belongs to the householder.
He remained silent.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having brought forth abundant gold by means of carts, loads, baskets, bags, camels, oxen, and donkeys,
began to cover the entire Jeta Grove;
yet it was not finished.
"There still remains a certain portion of ground not yet covered";
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, reflecting on this matter, remained silent for a moment, thinking: "What could that treasure be?"
It should be neither too little nor too much, so that this uncovered portion of ground will be covered,
yet it shall not need to be guarded again.
Prince Jeta reflected:
"Surely the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is feeling regret;
why else would he give up such a vast heap of wealth for the sake of a grove?"
Having understood this, he said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"If you have regret, O householder, take back the gold;
the park is mine alone."
"Prince, I have no regret;
rather, it was while reflecting on this very matter that I remained silent for a moment:
which of those treasures will it be?"
It should be neither too little nor too much,
so that this uncovered portion of ground will be covered,
yet it shall not need to be preserved again.
Then this thought occurred to Prince Jeta:
"Surely the Buddha will not be inferior; the proclamation of the Dharma will not be inferior."
"Since this householder is now renouncing such a vast heap of wealth for the sake of a grove," having understood this, he said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, grant me a plot of ground that has not yet been covered."
"Here I shall have a gateway constructed for the sake of the Blessed One;
the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is offering to Prince Jeta a portion of ground not yet covered [with gold], where Prince Jeta may have a gateway constructed for the sake of the Blessed One."

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada began to have a monastery built for the sake of the Blessed One, the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthyas), their minds agitated by intense hatred, gathered together and approached the place where the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was.
Having approached him, they said:
"Householder, do not build a monastery here for the sake of the ascetic Gautama.
For what reason?"
The cities have been divided by us:
Rājagṛha belongs to the ascetic Gautama; Śrāvastī belongs to us.
He said: "The cities have been divided by you, but my own property has not."
"Whichever of you desires it, for him I shall have a division of the Dharma constructed.
They went into the presence of the king;
there too, they were defeated by Anāthapiṇḍada.
The crows—that is, the heretics with unaltered faces—said:
"Householder, we do not grant you your wish;
the foremost disciple of the ascetic Gautama has arrived."
"If he defeats us in debate,
then have a monastery built"; he replied:
"Excellent! I shall first seek out the noble Śāriputra.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the venerable Śāriputra;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the venerable Śāriputra and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, the non-Buddhist teachers say:
'Householder, we do not grant you the freedom to act as you wish.'"
"The foremost disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama has arrived;
if he defeats us in debate,
then have a monastery built."
"How should one proceed in this matter?
"Venerable Śāriputra," [he replied]. He saw that they existed; he saw that they were dependent upon him alone.
Again he reflects:
"Are my disciples who are to be trained by me limited to these alone, or are there others also to be trained through debate? He sees that there are;
he then considers, "After how long will they assemble? He sees.
"Upon the passing of seven days";
having reflected, he said:
"Householder, let it be so."
"But on the seventh day.
Thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, filled with joy and gladness, approached the non-Buddhist teachers; having approached them, he said this to the non-Buddhist teachers:
The Venerable Āryaśāriputra said: "Excellent;
let it be so;
however, on the seventh day."
They reflect:
"There must be one of two reasons for this;
either he wishes to flee."
Or perhaps he wishes to seek out an ally;
what is appropriate for this occasion?
We too shall seek out an ally.
They began to search for allies;
while searching for allies, they saw a wandering mendicant named Raktākṣa,
and they said to him:
"You are our fellow-celibate; you were summoned by us for debate with Śramaṇa Gautama as his chief disciple, yet you are now seeking out a partisan."
"Provide assistance for us;
after how much time?
On the seventh day from now; very well."
"So be it;
whenever you hold a gathering, you must inform me.
The heretics, their minds filled with apprehension and agitation, are searching for an opportunity day after day."
They were counting the days.
The non-Buddhists and Śāriputra contended until, on the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had a seat prepared upon a wide expanse of ground.
A lion throne was prepared for the venerable Śāriputra;
heretics dwelling in various countries had assembled,
as had the multitude of people residing in Śrāvastī and many hundreds of thousands of living beings dwelling in that vicinity.
Some had arisen out of curiosity,
while others were impelled by their previous roots of merit;

then the Venerable Śāriputra, escorted and surrounded by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his retinue, entered the circle of debaters, and having surveyed those to be trained, with a smile and with a perfectly tranquil deportment—
Having ascended the lion-throne, he sat down;
and that entire assembly sat with attentive minds, gazing intently at the Venerable Śāriputra.
The Defeat of the Tīrthyas.
Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the non-Buddhist teachers: "Sirs, what will you do?
Or rather, will you undo it?"
They said: "We shall do it;
you transform yourself."
The Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"If I were to perform this, even the world with its gods would not be able to undo it."
Knowing that the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa had already arrived, he said this to the wandering mendicant Raktākṣa: "You do it;
I shall transform it."
He was skilled in the art of sorcery;
by him, a mango tree in full bloom was conjured up;
the Venerable Śāriputra then released a violent wind and rain.
By which [power] he was uprooted along with his roots and scattered here and there, becoming beyond the reach even of practitioners of yoga;
then, by him, a lotus pond was created;
and by the Venerable Śāriputra, a young elephant was created.
He crushed her on all sides;
he then manifested a seven-headed naga;
the Venerable Śāriputra manifested a garuḍa.
By whomsoever he was carried off,
by him a vetāḍa was conjured;
the Venerable Śāriputra pinned it down with mantras.
A Vetāla misdirected causes its own destruction;
it rushed right upon him.
Then, terrified, trembling, agitated, and with his hair standing on end, he fell at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra.
"Noble Śāriputra, protect me! I have come to you for refuge.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra neutralized the mantras;
that vetāḍa was pacified.
The Venerable Śāriputra taught him the Dharma; having conceived faith, he said:
"Noble Śāriputra, may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
"I shall practice the holy life in the presence of the noble Śāriputra.
The venerable Śāriputra ordained him, conferred full admission upon him, and gave him instruction.

Then, by striving, exerting himself, and making an effort, through the abandonment of all defilements, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste, having burst the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the analytical insights, and the higher faculties, and turned his back on existence, gain, and desire.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra;
thereupon, that assembly, their eyes wide with wonder,
became full of faith toward the Venerable Śāriputra and said:
Having understood that the great bull among speakers had been defeated by the noble Śāriputra, they all turned their gaze toward the face of the venerable Śāriputra.

Then, the venerable Śāriputra, having discerned the inclinations, latent tendencies, elements, and natures of that assembly, delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths such that—
Having heard this, many thousands of beings attained great distinction;
some resolved their minds upon the enlightenment of a disciple (śrāvaka-bodhi), and others upon solitary enlightenment (pratyeka-bodhi).
Some resolved upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment;
some took up the precepts for going for refuge;
and someone realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Some realized the fruit of once-returning; some, the fruit of non-returning;
and some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the complete abandonment of all afflictions.
For the most part, that assembly was inclined toward the Buddha,
leaning toward the Dharma,
and tending toward the Saṅgha.
[The matter] was settled;
the non-Buddhist teachers reflected:
"It is not possible for us to defeat him in debate."
"A stratagem must be devised;
let us work here for wages, and then, having found an opportunity, we shall have him killed by a hired murderer."
They all went together to the presence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and said:
"Householder, you have cut off all our means of livelihood;
therefore, please show us compassion."
"We shall perform work for hire in your monastery;
we have resided here for a long time,
so let us not abandon this country."
Anāthapiṇḍada said,
"I shall first look for the noble Śāriputra";
he then approached the venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Noble One,
the non-Buddhists say that you have cut off all our means of livelihood."
Therefore, have compassion;
let us perform work for hire in your monastery,
for we have resided here for a long time.
"We shall not abandon the region.
The Venerable Śāriputra then began to reflect: "Do they possess any roots of merit, or do they not? He saw that they did.
"They exist; to whom are they bound?
To me alone.
Having reflected thus, he says:
"Householder, let it be so;
what contradiction is there in this?
Thus they began to perform labor in that monastery for wages.
The venerable Śāriputra manifested a fierce man as a whip-bearer;
he began to compel them to perform that labor.
Knowing it was the time for their conversion, the venerable Śāriputra stood nearby at the foot of a tree, walking back and forth.
He was seen by them;
they reflected,
"This is the time to kill him, for he stands in a secluded place."
Having approached him, they stood surrounding him;
the Venerable Śāriputra reflected:
"With what kind of intention have these people come into my presence?"
When he saw that they were intent on killing him, he released that created being, the cane-guardian;
by him they were driven away with the words, "Go! Perform your work!"
They said:
"Noble Śāriputra, save us!
He replied:
"Venerable one, go;
let them rest for now.
They reflected:
"Such is this Great Being;
we were intent on his death,
yet he possesses a mind of loving-kindness toward us"— having realized this, they became filled with serene faith.

Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, having understood their intentions, latent tendencies, elements, and dispositions, delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Upon hearing it, they shattered with the vajra of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, they said:
"May we, Śāriputra, obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya;
may we, Venerable Śāriputra, practice the holy life under you. Thus they were granted the going forth and the full ordination by the Venerable Śāriputra.
Instruction was given; by them, applying themselves and striving, [it was practiced].

Striving diligently, they understood this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable; having struck down all conditioned states by realizing their nature as subject to decay, falling, scattering, and destruction, they realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements and thus became arhats.

Free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with minds like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, they have burst the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights, and have turned their backs on existence, gain, greed, and honor.
They became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Indra.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra took up the measuring cord for the monastery in a secluded spot.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada also took hold of him by one side;
the Venerable Śāriputra began to manifest a smile,
whereupon the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"Noble Śāriputra, Tathāgatas or the disciples of a Tathāgata do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Noble Śāriputra, what is the cause? What is the condition for manifesting this smile?"
"So it is, householder;
so it is. Tathāgatas or the disciples of a Tathāgata do not manifest a smile without cause or condition. And you have here taken up this sutra."
In the Tuṣita host of gods, a golden mansion has appeared;
then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, his eyes wide with wonder, said:
"Noble Śāriputra, if it is so..."
"In that case, spread the cloth once more so that it is even greater;
I wish to clear my mind.
The Venerable Śāriputra took up that cloth.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s mind was further gladdened by an even more intense surge of serene faith;
as soon as that faith arose, that golden mansion immediately became composed of the four jewels,
and this was reported to him by the Venerable Śāriputra.
Then, by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, whose succession of merit had increased ever further, sixteen great monasteries were constructed;
sixty small dwellings were also built.
Having had the sixteen great monasteries and the sixty small dwellings constructed and having filled them with all necessary requisites, he approached the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having approached, he said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, by how many stages of travel does the Blessed One proceed on the road?
It is just like that of a universal monarch, householder."
"By what measure does a wheel-turning monarch travel?

Householder, a wheel-turning monarch travels the road by ten-krośa stages. Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada calculated the halting places along the route between Śrāvastī and Rājagṛha and had rest-houses constructed.
A hall for giving was constructed; a man was appointed as the announcer of the time;
and archways were erected, adorned with parasols, banners, and flags, sprinkled with sandalwood water, and hung with censers of fragrant incense.
Medicines for both immediate and delayed administration have been prepared.
Then, having gathered his provisions, he addressed a certain man: "Messenger to the Buddha," he said.
"Come, sir; go to where the Blessed One is.
Having approached, bow at the feet of the Blessed One in our name and inquire after his freedom from illness and his freedom from affliction."
Ease of rising, mobility,
strength,
happiness, and blamelessness.
and for a dwelling in comfort;
and speak thus:
"May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī."
"I shall attend upon the Blessed One for as long as I live with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of monks.
"So be it, Noble One," that man replied to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and set out for Rājagṛha.
Gradually he arrived at Rājagṛha;
then, having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.

Standing to one side, that man said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One; [as before] up to: and for the sake of dwelling in comfort."
"May you be happy, O man, as well as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada!
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, venerable sir, says this:
'May the Blessed One come to Śrāvastī.'"
"I shall attend upon the Blessed One for as long as life lasts with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented to that man by remaining silent.
Then, perceiving the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, that man bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed from his presence.
The Buddha arrived at Śrāvastī;
then the Blessed One was self-subdued and surrounded by a retinue that was self-subdued, he was peaceful and surrounded by a retinue that was peaceful.
He is liberated, with a retinue that is liberated; he is comforted, with a retinue that is comforted;
he is disciplined, with a retinue that is disciplined.
An Arhat with an entourage of Arhats, one free from passion with an entourage free from passion,
one who is serene with a serene entourage.
Like a bull surrounded by a herd of cows,
like an elephant surrounded by its calves,
like a lion surrounded by a pack of fanged beasts.
Like a swan surrounded by a flock of swans,
like a garuḍa surrounded by a flock of birds,
like a brahmin surrounded by a group of disciples.

He was like a physician surrounded by a multitude of patients; like a hero surrounded by a host of warriors; like a guide surrounded by a multitude of travelers; like a caravan leader surrounded by a group of merchants; like a guild-master surrounded by his attendants;

like a provincial king surrounded by a council of ministers; like a universal monarch surrounded by a thousand sons; like the moon surrounded by a host of stars; like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays; [like] Dhṛtarāṣṭra...
Like a Gandharva surrounded by a host of Gandharvas, like Virūḍhaka surrounded by a host of Kumbhāṇḍas, like Virūpākṣa surrounded by a host of Nāgas, like Dhanada surrounded by a host of Yakṣas,

like Vemacitrin surrounded by a host of Asuras, like Śakra surrounded by a host of the Thirty-three Gods, like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmakāyika gods, he was like a tranquil ocean, like a rain-cloud laden with water, like a lordly elephant free from rut— with his senses perfectly subdued.

His movement and conduct were undisturbed; he was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics, his form graced by a fathom-wide halo, and his radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns.
Like a moving mountain of jewels, he was auspicious on all sides, endowed with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion.

Followed by the community of monks, by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada together with his retinue, by the multitude of people residing in Śrāvastī, and by many hundreds of thousands of deities, [he entered] the city of Śrāvastī.
He arrived;
and when the Blessed One, upon entering the city of Śrāvastī, deliberately placed his right foot upon the threshold of the city gate, a sixfold earthquake occurred.
This great earth shakes, trembles, and quakes;
it stirs, is agitated, and is thoroughly shaken;
the eastern quarter rises while the western quarter sinks.
The west rises and the east sinks;
the south rises and the north sinks;
the north rises and the south sinks.
The edges rose up while the center sank;
the center rose up while the edges sank.

And this entire world, together with the intermediate spaces between worlds, became suffused with a sublime radiance, and in the sky the divine drums resounded, while deities stationed in the expanse of the firmament [honored] the Blessed One.

From above, they began to scatter divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and white lotuses; they scattered powdered aloe-wood, powdered saffron, and *tamāla* leaves; they threw down divine *māndāraka* flowers and waved their garments.
The effects felt following the Buddha’s arrival:
Upon the Blessed One’s entry into the city, these and other such wonders occurred:

narrow spaces became wide, low places became high, and high places became level; elephants trumpeted, horses neighed, bulls bellowed, and various musical instruments within the houses sounded of their own accord.
The blind regain their sight, the deaf their hearing, and the mute become capable of speech;
those with impaired remaining faculties recover them;
and those overcome by the intoxication of liquor become sobered.
Those who have been made to drink poison become free from poison;
those who are mutual enemies attain friendliness;
and pregnant women give birth safely.
Those bound by fetters are released; the destitute [become] wealthy.
They obtain these and other hundreds of thousands of wonders that manifest when the Blessed One enters a city.
Then the Blessed One entered Śrāvastī with such great honor;
having entered, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, surrounded by his friends, kinsmen, and relatives, took up a golden pitcher and began to pour a stream of water;
yet it did not fall.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, being dejected, reflected:
"I have not performed any actions that are accompanied by faults; rather, while you were standing in this spot, you dedicated this place to the former Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Stand in another spot and strike it.
By him—
Standing in another place,
[the sound] was cast forth;
the Blessed One himself proclaimed the Jeta Grove with a voice endowed with five qualities.
While the name of Jetavana was being proclaimed, Prince Jeta thought:
"Oh, would that the Blessed One would mention my name first!
Perceiving Prince Jeta's thought with his own mind, the Blessed One mentioned him first.
"Monks, this is Jetavana, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Upon hearing this, Prince Jeta was deeply inspired with faith, thinking, "The Blessed One has mentioned my name first of all.
Filled with joy and gladness, he had a gateway made of the four precious substances constructed for the sake of the Blessed One using all that wealth.
Likewise, the Elder compilers of the scriptures also recorded in the Sūtra: "The Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts, regarding the previous births of Anāthapiṇḍada during the time of the seven Buddhas.
"Venerable sir, where was this plot of ground previously offered by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to former perfectly enlightened Buddhas?
The Blessed One said:

"In the past, monks, ninety-one aeons ago, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Vipaśyin appeared in the world, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed."
The Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
arrived at this place surrounded by a retinue of sixty-two thousand monks.
At that time, there was in Śrāvastī a householder named Tiṣya.
Therefore, having covered another area six *krośas* with gold and bullion and purchased it from the prince, he offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin;
having gone forth in his very presence, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements.
The nephew of the householder Tiṣya, through association with him, became exceedingly devoted to the Tathāgata Vipaśyin.
He had a stūpa for the hair and nails of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin constructed;

he reflected, "What means might there be by which I may see this [stūpa] both by night and by day without it being obscured? A disciple of his, staying on the seashore, sent to him a radiant jewel that was enveloped in light.
He placed it upon that stūpa;
seeing this, he was filled with faith and made a formal aspiration:

"Just as this plot of ground was purchased by my maternal uncle from the prince and, having been covered with gold and silver, was offered to the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipaśyin; even so, may I cover this plot of ground with gold and silver and offer it to the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
And when he who is the last of them has appeared, may I go forth into homelessness in his presence and, through the abandonment of all defilements, realize arhatship."
What do you think, monks?
That nephew of the householder at that time and on that occasion was none other than this householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Thenceforward, in the thirty-first aeon, a teacher named Śikhin appeared in the world, as previously described, up until: he was a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Accompanied by a retinue of sixty thousand bhikṣus, he arrived at this place.
At that time, there was a householder named Puṣya;
he covered this area of earth for two and a half krośas with jewels, purchased it from the prince, and offered it to the Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikhin together with his community of disciples.
"Monks, it may be that you think, 'At that time, on that occasion, was he perhaps some other householder named Puṣya?
But it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, it was this very same householder Anāthapiṇḍada who, at that time, on that occasion, was [Puṣya]."
Prior to that, in that very thirty-first eon, a teacher named Viśvabhū appeared in the world, as previously described, up until: he was a Buddha, a Blessed One;
accompanied by a retinue of sixty thousand monks, he arrived at this location.
At that time, there was a householder named Māgha.

Therefore, having covered this area for two *krośas* with pearls and having purchased it from the prince, he offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One Viśvabhū together with his community of disciples.
"Monks, you might think that at that time, on that occasion, the householder named Māghu was someone else.
But it should be seen thus: it was none other than this very householder Anāthapiṇḍada who, at that time, on that occasion, was Māghu."
Prior to that, in this Bhadraka Kalpa, a teacher named Krakutsunda appeared in the world—a Buddha, a Blessed One—as previously described;
he arrived at this place accompanied by a retinue of forty thousand monks.
At that time, there was a householder named Bhavadatta.
He also filled this area with cattle and, having brought it forth from the presence of the prince, offered it to the perfectly enlightened Krakucchanda together with his community of disciples.
"Monks, you might think that at that time and on that occasion, the householder named Bhavadatta was someone else;
however, you should not view it in that way."
Moreover, it was this very same householder Anāthapiṇḍada at that time and on that occasion.

Subsequently, in this very Bhadraka Kalpa, when the lifespan of beings was thirty thousand years, a teacher named Kanakamuni appeared in the world—as described before—up until: he was a Buddha, a Blessed One;
accompanied by a retinue of thirty thousand monks, he arrived at this very spot.
At that time, there was a householder named Bṛhaspati;
he too, having spread this area with cloth and purchased it from the prince, offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One Kanakamuni together with his community of disciples.
It may well be that...
"O monks, do you think that at that time and on that occasion, the householder named Bṛhaspati was anyone else?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way."
Moreover, it was this very same householder Anāthapiṇḍada at that time and on that occasion.

Subsequently, in this very Bhadraka Kalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Kāśyapa appeared in the world—as previously described—up until: he, the Buddha, the Blessed One, arrived at this very spot accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand.
At that time, there was a householder named Āṣāḍha; he,
having covered this area of ground for half a krośa with golden barley, purchased it from the Prince and offered it to the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa together with his community of disciples.
"Perhaps, monks, it might occur to you that the householder named Āṣāḍha at that time and on that occasion was someone else?"
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, that very householder Anāthapiṇḍada was he at that time and on that occasion.

And now, monks, I have arisen in the world as the Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the worlds, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
The Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Blessed One;
I too have arrived at this place with a retinue of twelve hundred and fifty.

Now, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having covered the ground with a layer of sixteen thousand gold coins from the plowshares, has purchased [the grove] from Prince Jeta for me and my community of disciples.
It has been offered.
Monks, in the future, when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, a teacher named Maitreya will come to this place, accompanied by a retinue of ninety-six thousand koṭis of arhats.
At that time, there will arise a householder named Sudhana.
He too, having covered this area for three *yojanas* with gold and fine gold, will purchase it from the youth and present it to Maitreya together with his community of disciples;
having gone forth in that very teaching, he will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
Now, monks, could it be that at that time and on that occasion, the householder named Sudhana was someone else?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way;
rather, this very same householder Anāthapiṇḍada will arise as the householder named Sudhana. Anāthapiṇḍada possesses the power to perceive hidden treasures.

Whether near or far, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw treasures—both those with owners and those without owners, those situated on land and those situated in water; those that were distant and those that were nearby.
A report spread throughout the vicinity: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada sees treasures, including those with owners."
"Even those that are ownerless, whether on land or in water, whether far away or near at hand.
Now at that time, many various heterodox śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, carakas, and parivrājakas were seated together and assembled in the hall of curiosity, and among them this kind of discussion arose:
A conversation arose among them:
"By what characteristic, sirs, is the householder Anāthapiṇḍada endowed that he sees treasures— whether they have an owner or no owner, whether they are situated on land or in water,
and whether they are far away or near?"
At that time, a young brahmin named Upagu was seated and present in that very assembly;
he said:
"May you all, sirs, be free from anxiety."

"I shall deliberate and tell you by what characteristic the householder Anāthapiṇḍada perceives treasures— whether they have an owner or are ownerless, whether they are situated on land or in water, and whether they are far or near.
Thus intent on tracking the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s movements and habits, he followed closely behind him until, at another time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was at the Ajiravatī River.
Having bathed, he emerged;
[the monk] struck him on the back with his palm;
the householder Anāthapiṇḍada remained silent even as he watched.
He said:

"Householder, you are known to be endowed with patience and gentleness; it is because of this that you see treasures—whether they have an owner or are ownerless, whether they are on land or in water, and whether they are far away or near."
He informed the non-Buddhist teachers;
the non-Buddhist teachers, boasting as well, announced it everywhere;
thus the report spread throughout the countryside.

Now, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was endowed with patience and gentleness such that he could see treasures— whether they had an owner or were ownerless, whether they were situated on land or in water, and whether they were far away or near.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it is not easy for even hundreds of thousands of millions of non-Buddhist heretics to understand by what characteristic the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is endowed so that he sees treasures.
