Rather, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada has a treasury with a variegated interior of jewels; he is a lord of gold, and by means of this [power], he sees treasures—whether they have an owner or are ownerless, whether they are situated on land or in water, whether they are far away or near."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the ripening of which resulted in his becoming one whose inner treasury was variegated with jewels and who was a lord of gold?
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada alone; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and they are inevitable.
Who else shall experience the actions performed and accumulated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth-element."

They ripen neither in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; rather, deeds performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Deeds do not perish even in hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.

The Story of the Pratyekabuddha (concerning a previous life of Anāthapiṇḍada): "Long ago, monks, in a certain mountain village there lived a householder who was wealthy, of great fortune and great enjoyment, possessing vast and extensive estates, endowed with wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa,
and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa."

When the spring season had arrived, and the trees were in full bloom, while the forest grove resounded with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and pheasants, he went out to the park grounds together with his retinue.

At times when Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas arise; they are compassionate toward the lowly and the wretched, devoted to remote dwellings and lodgings, and are the sole objects of veneration for the world.
Meanwhile, a certain pratyekabuddha, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that small village;
he stayed in a certain spot within that park,
and the park keeper informed the householder:
"Now, in that place, a tranquil-souled renunciant resides";
upon hearing this, joy arose within him. "I am fortunate indeed," he thought, "that such a renunciant dwells in my park. Having conceived this faith, he set out to see him.

That Great Being, having entered the realm of nirvana without remainder, passed away; thereupon, that householder, together with his friends, kinsmen, relatives, and household members, cremated him with great honor,
and the funeral pyre was extinguished with milk.
Those bones were mixed with jewels and placed inside a crystal jar;
remaining within it, they shone forth and produced a sound.
Then, prostrating at his feet, he made this aspiration:
"Just as his bones, interspersed with jewels, shine exceedingly and emit a sound, even so, by this root of merit, may I have a treasury with a variegated interior of jewels and be a lord of gold.
What do you think, monks?
The householder who was at that time and on that occasion was none other than this very householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Because he performed a service for a pratyekabuddha and made a vow, and because— as the nephew of the householder Tiṣya— he placed a jewel that emitted light upon the hair-and-nail stūpa of the perfectly awakened Buddha Vipaśyin, through the ripening of that karma, he became one whose inner treasury is variegated with jewels and a lord of gold.
"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed.

Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Having abandoned black actions and those that are mixed, we shall apply ourselves only to entirely white actions. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
The intermediate summary verse: Tiṣya, Puṣya, Māghu, Bhavadatta, Bṛhaspati,
Āṣāḍha, Sudatta, and Sudhana is the last.
Gold, fine gold, and pearls as the third;
with cows, cloths, and barley, ten million [gifts] were offered, elevated by gold.

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having spread out a layer of crores [of gold coins], purchased [the park] from Prince Jeta and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, then faithful people dwelling in various countries went to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the caitya.
Some among them, being full of faith, said:
"Noble one, we too would like to have some building constructed in the Jeta Grove for the noble ones' use.
The monks said:
"Having purchased the land for a price, have it built.
"Noble sir, for how much price is it given? "For this much gold."
"Noble one, how could we have so much? Nevertheless, if we obtain it in this place, we shall do so.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"The householder must be consulted;
if he gives permission, it may be carried out."
The monks looked toward the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; he said:
"In my name, faithful brahmins and householders perform meritorious deeds for the sake of the Saṅgha; I authorize this."
“They do it for the person; I do not permit this.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
Therefore, I authorize that it may be constructed for the sake of the Saṃgha;
for the sake of an individual, the donor must be consulted;
if he authorizes it, it may be constructed.
He did not permit it,
saying, "It must not be done.
Then, some visiting monks who had come to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the caitya arrived.
Just as they had entered into the presence of the monks through mutual acquaintance,
others who lacked such acquaintances were frustrated;
regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
"A place not specifically assigned should be set aside for the sake of visiting monks.
In a certain mountain retreat there was a monastery;
there, the monks entered the rainy season retreat.
When danger arose in that mountain village during the rainy season, the monks residing there became terrified; being uninvited, they came to Śrāvastī.
Having been received by the monks there, and once their fatigue from the journey had been dispelled, they said:
"Venerable ones, designate the lodgings!
But they, thinking it was during the rainy season, did not designate them;
consequently, the visiting monks criticized, reviled, and censured them.

"How is it, venerable ones, that you are now causing the disappearance of the Teacher's very teaching while he himself still stands? If you have any remorse, assign the lodgings according to seniority!
Even so, they did not assign them.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that for the sake of monks who have broken their [vows] or are broken [in conduct], a second invitation for the rains retreat (varṣopanāyikā) should be performed."
The monks did not know how it should be performed;
the Blessed One said:
"Regarding the three-month period":
it was said by the Blessed One,
"For the sake of those monks whose [robes] have been torn apart, a second invitation for the rains retreat (varṣopanāyikā) should be performed."
Meanwhile, other monks who had been defeated by various stratagems also arrived at Śrāvastī;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:

"O monks, it was on account of those monks who were defeated by various stratagems that I established a second invitation for the rains-retreat, but not a third; yet those monks defeated by stratagems should be granted rest according to their acquaintance with one another.
However, the monks are making them perform manual labor."
The Blessed One said:
"They must not be made to undertake [monastic] duties";
yet the monks continued to provide them with their share of gains.
The Blessed One said: "No gain should be given to them;
even the monks do not provide them with material gains."
The Blessed One said:
"They receive gains of material goods, but not gains of robes.
Then, the faithful caused many monasteries to be built.
In Śrāvastī, few monks entered the rains retreat;
they remained in empty dwellings, and thus the donors did not obtain merit resulting from the use [of their offerings].
They were being inhabited by sons of Māra;
the Blessed One said:
"All should be assigned; for each individual, two, three, or four should be assigned according to their capacity, and all should be used."
In some cases one should remain in the forenoon, in some at midday, and in others in the afternoon.
"In some cases, one must stay overnight";
however, those monks did not perform the ritual action and were thus deceived.
The Blessed One said:
The donor should be encouraged; it is good if he indeed succeeds in doing so. If he does not succeed, they should be restored using property belonging to the Saṃgha.
"If it is not possible [to ordain all], then the formal ritual (*saṃskāra*) should be performed for as many as is possible,
while others should be disregarded.
At that time, when the Blessed One's teaching had become widespread, many monks arrived at Śrāvastī.
They were troubled regarding their lodgings;
the Blessed One said:

"It should be assigned to two or three, or at least to all of them collectively, according to the space available for sitting; the location for the water-jars, the place for drinking water, the medicine, the tooth-sticks, and the bowls [should also be assigned]."
Having excluded [that]; and mutual courtesy (*sāmīcī*) is indeed common etiquette (*upacāra*), so it should not be specifically prescribed.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
Meditate, monks, on various forest retreats, at the roots of trees, in empty dwellings, in mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, woods, and remote lodgings;
do not be negligent.
"Lest you later come to feel regret";
thus was the praise of the forest-dwelling life spoken of in many ways.
Then, some monks, having undertaken the practice of forest-dwelling, settled in the wilderness.
There they were robbed by thieves;
having been robbed, while seeking robes from the families of brahmins and householders, they neglected their instruction, recitation, study, yoga, and mental attention.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"A dwelling place should be established for the sake of forest-dwelling monks";
thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
"A dwelling should be established for the sake of forest-dwelling monks.
The monks established it in a place that was not well-lit.
A forest-dwelling monk, having set down his bowl and robe, closed the door, took a staff, and departed.
"The dwelling of other forest-dwelling monks must be set aside.
Now, a certain householder had built a monastery for Upananda,
but he did not reside there.
When a visiting monk arrived, [the resident] gave him lodging but took the gains for himself;
this continued until a monk who possessed only the three robes (traicīvarika) arrived. That monk saw the monastery was empty.
He asks, "To whom does this monastery belong?
and the monks reply:
[It was] of the monk Upananda;
he went and requested it from him,
and he said:
"This is a monastery; dwell here; whatever gain there is in this shall be mine";
he remained there.
Therefore, that monastery was never swept, nor was a fine coating of cow dung ever applied;
eventually, he departed from that monastery.
Another monk arrived;
he too, having requested [lodging] from Upananda, stayed in that monastery;
he saw that monastery filled with refuse.
Having cleared away the refuse and taken up a broom, he swept it clean and stood near a refuse heap;
then, being seen by a certain monk, the latter said:
"Venerable one, why do you stand here with a broom held in your hand; is this broom not to be set down?
He replied:
"Someone here was stationed as a hand-guard; therefore, he never once even set down his broom. He said:
"A certain monk who possesses only the three robes is staying here";
meanwhile, as he was wandering for alms, he saw him and reproached him, whereupon he said:
“Upananda takes the gain; I shall clean his dwelling.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"Whoever receives the gains must sweep the monastery";
thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"The dedication of offerings (dakṣiṇā) should be performed in the name of deceased donors."
The senior of the Saṃgha recited a verse for the sake of the donors who had passed away;
a certain householder came to the monastery and heard it.
He assigned the dedication of the gift;
he approached that person and said,
"Noble sir, if I have a monastery built, will you also dedicate the gift in my name?"
He said, "Build it well; I shall give you instructions.
Thereupon, that householder had a monastery constructed.
In that matter, he had given nothing at all;
he remained entirely empty,
until he was seen by that householder.
Having arrived at the monastery, he said: "Venerable sir, my monastery stands empty; no monk resides there."
The elder of the Saṃgha said: "Worthy sir, it must be steamed. That householder replied:
"Noble one, it was built on saline, barren ground; how can it be heated?
"Householder, I did not say this with that in mind; rather, I meant that there is no profit to be gained there."
He said:
"Noble one, whoever now resides in my monastery, him I shall clothe with a robe; thus, profit is obtained. Thinking this, Upananda gradually took possession of it as if it were his own share.
He continued to dwell in that very same place;
it remained empty until a certain alms-collector, who was devoted to visiting shrines, arrived at Śrāvastī.
He saw that monastery was empty;
he asked the monks: "To whom does this monastery belong?"
Thus they replied: "This monastery belongs to the Saṅgha, but it has been assigned to the monk Upananda. He then approached Upananda.
"This monastery has been assigned to you; I shall stay here.
He replied, "Do so."
He remained there;
being an alms-collector who was skillful and diligent,
he made that place smeared and swept every day.
There are five advantages in sweeping:
one's own mind becomes serene;
the mind of another becomes serene; and the deities become joyful.
He accumulates roots of merit conducive to a beautiful appearance;
at the breaking up of the body, he will be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world among the gods.
Those who see that monastery plastered and swept go and inform the householder of this.
Having heard this, he felt great joy;
then, at another time, having come there himself, he saw that very same monastery smeared and swept clean,
and he was filled with serene faith.
By that [means], the alms-collector was covered by the cloth;
Upananda heard of it and went there with great haste, saying:
"This monastery has been assigned to me as an alms-food eater;
give me a cloth," [said the donor].
The alms-food eater reflected:
"If this is for the sake of profit, even so he will seize it by force and expel me from the monastery";
thus he handed it over to him.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"To whomsoever he is pleased, for him alone does he perform the act of favor;
however, the gain of Upānanda belongs to the rainy season."
The world is fond of virtue; even by afflicting themselves, their sons, and their wives, faithful brahmins and householders bestow gifts upon those possessed of virtue;
they invite forest-dwelling monks and provide them with a meal.
While forest-dwelling monks had gone to eat inside a house, their monasteries were plundered by thieves;
the Blessed One said:
"Having bolted the door and taken the key, one should depart."
Thieves who take what is not given were stealing by means of false keys;
the Blessed One said:
"One should go after having stationed a monk as a guard."
"One should ensure that he has no lack of alms-food";
[thinking this,] those who take what is not given go along taking another monk with them; he says:
"Open the door," [he said].
The Blessed One replied:
"One must discern whether it is with fever or free from fever."
If he says, "I am feverish," he must not be released;
but if he says, "I am free from fever," he should be released.
Nevertheless, a forest-dwelling monk should provide a half-branch (for support).
The Blessed One said:
"A forest-dwelling monk should maintain a 'half-branch' (ardhaśākhā).
The monks did not know what kind of thing a half-branch was.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, the dog is the 'half-branch'; the remains from his alms-bowl should be given to him.
The forest-dwelling monks then kept dogs as companions.
They scratched the courtyard and the monastery grounds with their claws and defiled them with excrement and urine.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, I shall prescribe the rules of customary conduct for a monk who keeps dogs."
A monk who keeps dogs must rise early in the morning and inspect the courtyard of the stūpa and the monastery;
whatever has been scratched by their claws should be smoothed over,
and the excrement and urine should be cleared away.
If a monk who keeps dogs as pets fails to undertake and abide by the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed,
he acts with transgression.
The Venerable Upananda was the senior of the Saṅgha in a certain monastery;
then, another senior of the Saṅgha arrived there,
and Upananda reflected:
"Having been the senior elder of the Saṅgha in this monastery, I must become the second elder;
I shall go to another monastery.
He then went to another monastery.
Then he departed from that monastery;
whatever was the gain belonging to the second elder there became the property of the community elder.
He reflected:
"Even here,
that same gain is mine; even there, that same gain was mine."

"Why should I take on the position of the senior monk of the Saṃgha without a purpose? he thought; then, hurrying as quickly as possible, he set out for the monastery and entered it when half of the bedding and seats had already been assigned.
He said:
"Assign the monastery according to seniority.
The monks, considering that [the time] had passed, did not assign it.
Upananda said:
"Venerable ones, why do you let the Teacher's dispensation perish while it still stands?
Assign the monastery according to seniority!"
The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:
"Whoever [uses] what belongs to the Saṃgha or what belongs to a stūpa..."
When one has gone for some business, the lodgings must be assigned according to seniority;
otherwise, they are to be assigned according to the order of arrival.

Upananda, out of excessive greed, entered the rains retreat in two monasteries, thinking he would receive the gains from both. When the rains were completed, he sought the gain, but it was not obtained there.
Nor did he do so toward another;
he reviled the monks who were assigned to the lodgings.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Since he has completed the rains retreat, his share of gains should be given to him.
The monks then gave [the gains] from both monasteries as well.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, one should not give from both dwellings;
they should give from only one."
Other monks reproached, censured, and spoke against this, saying:
"Why is it given from one [monastery] when he has spent the rains retreat in both monasteries? The monks reported that matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Even from both monasteries, half of half [the portion] should be given to the deity;
furthermore, a monk must not enter two monasteries."
They approach [the monks], and they become guilty of an offense of transgression.
A certain householder had two monasteries built.
One [robe] was for the forest-dwellers, the second for those living near the villages;
it was the custom of that householder to clothe each individual monk of the Saṅgha who had completed the rainy-season retreat with a garment.
Taking his cloths, he set out for the forest monastery;
Upananda heard that a share of the monastery was being granted in the forest.
He sent a message to Nanda, saying,
"If any gain is offered here, you shall take it," and having said this, he set out in haste for the forest monastery;
he was seen by that householder.
He reflected:
"From the way he steps,
this man has gone to the forest monastery."
"What is appropriate here at this time?
I shall first give it right here in this village monastery,
and afterwards I will give it there."
Having turned back, he began to distribute the cloths;
Nanda extended his hand,
and the householder gave him a cloth.
He extended it further;
the householder said, "Noble sir, the cloth has been given to you."
"Why do you stretch it out further? He replied: "Householder, he says:"
"Noble sir, giving with one's own hand is praised by the Blessed One;
I shall give with my very own hand.
He stood silent, feeling ashamed.
Upananda reflected:
"That householder is taking a long time;
I shall go to the monastery in the vicinity of the village. Having realized this, he went to the monastery in the vicinity of the village and asked Nanda:
"Noble one, was my cloth taken?
He related exactly what had occurred;
the householder also went by another path to the forest monastery, distributed the cloths, and departed.
Upananda again rushed toward the forest monastery,
until his robes were stripped away.
Because of excessive greed for gain in both types of dwellings, he fell away from his acquisitions;
he grieved, was exhausted, and lamented.
The monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Venerable Upananda, see how he has fallen from his cloth due to excessive greed.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, this man brought about the interruption of a meal because of excessive greed."
Listen to that.
Once upon a time, monks, on both banks of a river there were two monasteries. Regarding the story of the dog who was too greedy (a previous birth of Upānanda): [the text continues].
One was for those who receive alms from the community, and the second was for those who live on alms;
meanwhile, a certain dog became accustomed to the sound of the gong.
Having heard the sound of the gong, he goes to the monastery of those who receive alms from the Saṅgha;
those monks give him the remains of their bowls, and having consumed that, he goes to the monastery of those who live on alms-food.
There too, having eaten the remnants from their alms-bowls, they departed as they pleased; then, at another time, when alms-food was obtained for those who were spontaneously born,
they struck the wooden gong at the proper hour.
That dog Gaṇḍī, upon hearing the sound of the gong, began to cross the river;
when he had reached midstream, the gong was struck at the monastery by those receiving the alms of the Saṃgha,
and his enthusiasm broken, he began to turn back.
Carried far away by the current and fallen from both sides—
what do you think, monks?
That dog named Gaṇḍika at that time, on that occasion, was none other than this very Upananda.
Even then, he fell away from both through excessive greed;
even now, he has fallen away from both through excessive greed.
Therefore, monks, a monk must not practice excessive greed.
One who does so commits an offense of transgression (sātisāra).
The summary verse (uddāna):
Quarrel, sufficiency for the sick, and the time of night in Kāśi.
A tree, a bare ground, a grassy plot, and the concealment of those who divide [the alms].
Precautions to be taken against quarrelsome monks:
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"In such a case, when monks hear that other monks who are makers of strife are coming..."
"Bond-makers,
quarrel-mongers, litigants, and those who initiate legal disputes will reproach us and remind us, whether out of shamelessness or for the sake of gain;
how should they be dealt with by them?"
Upāli, when resident monks hear that quarrelsome monks are approaching, they should appoint three assigners of bedding and seats and six receivers of bedding and seats.
Who are the three assigners of lodgings?
They are the winter, the summer, and the rainy-season assigner.
Who are the six receivers of lodgings?
Every monastery is to be assigned, as well as every area surrounding the monastery; every enclosure and every area surrounding the enclosure; every grove and every area surrounding the grove.
If he says, "Assign a monastery," one should say, "This monastery has been assigned;
assign the vicinity of the monastery, this too has been assigned;
assign the courtyard, this too has been assigned; assign the vicinity of the courtyard, this too has been assigned."
"Point out a monastery; this one has been pointed out. Point out the vicinity of the monastery; this one too has been pointed out.
Being without a shelter and without a fixed abode, they [asked]: "Whom..."
They will not give rise to any fault;
thereafter, when their momentum has subsided, when the adversaries have departed, and when the enemies have gone, the beds and seats should be assigned according to seniority.
The Blessed One said:
"The bedding and seating should be assigned according to seniority.
[This concerns] the care of the sick monks and Upananda’s mischief once again.
At one time, there was a certain sick monk;
an elder monk arrived, and according to seniority, the latter’s dwelling was assigned to him.
He was entirely new [to the community];
he did not enter another dwelling;
he was addressed by that monk:
"Venerable one, this dwelling has been assigned to me;
please depart.
He replied, "I am ill."
"I shall go back to my own home; that monk is cruel;
he has been cast out by him and placed in a lotus pond."
When the brahmins and householders arrived at the monastery,
desiring to see him, they beheld that monk and said: "Noble one,"
"Has this monk passed away? "O gentle sirs, he has not passed away."
Now, why was it assigned here? An elder monk arrived,
and this cell belonging to him was assigned to him.
Therefore, he has been expelled from here and stationed here;
we, noble ones, while being householders, expel those who are sick from their homes out of a desire for protection, but you are renunciants.
"Your Teacher is compassionate;
how then can you expel one who is ill? They then reproached, reviled, and censured him.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this origin, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, a relinquishment of duties (vastuparihāra) should be granted to a sick monk."
The Blessed One said:
"Relief from duties regarding property should be granted to a sick monk.
The Venerable Upananda, however, made a sound of "hum" and remained silent.
Thinking, "I shall assign the lodgings within six or seven days," he remained there with a bandage bound around his foot.
The monks who were assigning the lodgings, considering him to be ill, assigned that cell to him.
Once the lodgings had been assigned, he removed the bandage from his foot and remained there.
Then he was asked by the monks who were visiting the sick: "Has the Elder's foot recovered?
He replied:
"Has it not been said by the Blessed One that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent?"
"Will my illness then become permanent?
They replied, "Venerable sir, you will soon be restored to health."
"Alas, I am ill with the fever of the eon!
he said;
he replied, "Do you wish to cast me into a ruined dwelling?"
The monks of little purpose reproached, reviled, and censured them, saying:
"How is it now that these monks, though not ill, accept the relinquishment of their dwellings?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this origin, the Blessed One said: "Therefore, monks, the relinquishment of property for one who is ill for the duration of a kalpa should not be given, nor should it be accepted by him."
If one does so, one incurs an offense of transgression. The various blessings for those men who master the Vinaya:
The summary verse for the six pentads is as follows:
"One's own virtuous conduct is placed foremost, and moreover, it is unattached."
Birth is born of light, and it is indeed an obstacle.
Having placed the offense last, the summary of the alms-gathering is extracted;
having placed the intermediate summary first, there is another, both internal and external to others.
Having been composed for the benefit of many people, this first pentad comes into being.
The Blessed One established the Sūtra and the Mātṛkā among gods and humans; the Sūtra [was established] among the Nāgas;
but the Vinaya—

"It is profound, appearing profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, possessing many hidden intentions, and connected with worldly terminology; monks, because of its profundity, its possession of many hidden intentions, and its connection with worldly terminology, they do not venture to recite this Vinaya."
This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): for whichever limb the teaching declines, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak in high praise of that very limb.
On this matter, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, there are five advantages for a person who is a bearer of the Vinaya."
Which five?
He is held in high esteem by the fourfold assembly;
his instruction and admonition are not dependent on others.
He becomes the bearer of the inner treasury of the perfectly awakened ones of the past, future, and present;
having reached the summit of other ascetics and brahmins, he stands there;
and he is engaged for the welfare and happiness of many people, for the sake of the endurance of the true Dharma.
The intermediate summary verse: one's own virtue, approaching, remorse, and being confident;
having established these together with the Dharma, the second pentad comes into being.
There are five further advantages for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are the five?
Their own aggregate of ethical discipline becomes well-guarded and well-protected.
He becomes one who is to be approached by the fourfold assembly;
he becomes a refuge for persons overcome by remorse;
he dwells in the midst of the Saṅgha with confidence.
One grasps the adversary’s own true dharma. The intermediate summary verse: non-attachment, the determination of meaning, and likewise the training rules.
And let there be two Ālokas as well; thus the third [section] consists of five verses.
There are five further benefits for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are the five?
He extracts the meaning without being entangled.
He becomes well-ascertained regarding the determination of the meaning;
his training rules are well-mastered;
and he dwells frequently with a mind filled with light.
He brings light to future generations.
The summary verse: Illumination, radiance, and splendor; with little concern and not empty.
There are five further benefits for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are these five?
The direction before me appears as if light has arisen, as if radiance has arisen, and as if brilliance has arisen.
I dwell with little concern in that direction,
and that direction appears to me as not empty in which a person who upholds the Vinaya resides.
(Summary verse)
"Origination, designation, and indeed non-designation;
rejection and authorization—this is the fifth pentad.
There are five other benefits in a person who upholds the Vinaya:
Which five?
He knows origination;
he knows designation.
He knows the provisional designation,
he knows the prohibition,
and he knows the permission.
Summary verse:
... there are five further advantages in a person who is a holder of the Vinaya;
what are the five?
He knows what is an obstacle, he knows what is not an obstacle,
and he gives instruction.
He gives instruction;
he is capable of taking on the responsibility of providing guidance for his co-residents and pupils.
Summary verse: [...]
There are five further advantages for a person who upholds the Vinaya;
what are the five?
He knows an offense.
He knows what is not an offense;
he knows what is grave; he knows what is light.
The recitation of the *Prātimokṣasūtra* has been taught to him in detail. Among them, Upāli is the foremost of those who master and know the Vinaya.
Because the Blessed One spoke in praise of the Vinaya, the elder monks, filled with enthusiasm, began to study the Vinaya.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli was preeminent among those skilled in the origins and causes of the Vinaya.
As the elder monks were beginning to teach the Vinaya with great reverence so that they might master it,
he became pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically exhausted.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers who inquire;
knowing, they ask,
for it is not those who do not know who ask.
They ask at the proper time; they do not ask when overcome by the wrong time; they ask what is connected with the goal.
They do not ask questions that are connected with what is unbeneficial;
for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have destroyed the bridge regarding questions connected with what is unbeneficial.
In this regard, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know the proper time for questions connected with what is beneficial.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asked the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why is the monk Upāli so pale, emaciated, weak, withered, and physically exhausted? He replied:
The Blessed One spoke in praise of the Vinaya, and having heard it, the most senior monks began to study the Vinaya with great enthusiasm.
The Venerable Upāli, thinking that the most senior monks were acquiring mastery of the Vinaya with reverence, began to teach it with due respect;
as a result, he became very pale and emaciated.
"Durbalaka" means one whose body has become withered;
regarding this birth, the Blessed One said:
"O monks, I shall now prescribe for a monk the rules of proper conduct regarding the giving of instruction."
The monk who gives the instruction should give the instruction while employing four noble postures:
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
The monk who receives the instruction should receive it while employing three noble postures: [walking, standing, and sitting].

If a monk who is receiving the recitation approaches a monk who is giving the recitation while the latter is walking, and he is junior, he should perform the proper salutation (*sāmīcī*), inquire after his physical well-being, bow his body,
and with an upright mind and reverence, receive the recitation by stepping back;
however, if he is senior, [the procedure is as follows].

Having asked about his physical well-being and having bowed down to him, he should receive the formal instruction with an upright mind and with reverence, proceeding by stepping back with each foot. If the senior comes while he is standing and he is junior, he should perform the ritual salutation (*sāmīcī*), ask about his well-being, and then— having either squatted or sat on a lower seat— with an upright mind and with reverence, he should receive the formal instruction.

Now, if he is elderly, having asked whether his elements are in equilibrium, he should stand in a squatting position or sit on a lower seat; with a straight mind and with reverence, the instruction should be received.
Just as it is for one standing, so should it be applied for one sitting or lying down.
The monk who gives the instruction should give the instruction after having made it well-practiced, well-mastered, and free from doubt.
The one receiving the recitation should receive it only after having asked well, grasped it thoroughly, and made it free from doubt;
if the monk who gives the recitation and the one who receives the recitation do not proceed by undertaking the rules of conduct as they have been prescribed, they both become guilty of an offense.

While wandering on a journey through the countryside, the six monks of the group of six (ṣaḍvargikā bhikṣavaḥ) arrived at a monastery at night and were accommodated by the monks according to their acquaintances;
they said:
"Venerable ones, why do you stand here? Summon the assigner of lodgings. They asked, "For what purpose?
[He replied,] "To assign the lodgings."
They said, "The bedding is comfortable; you shall sleep well and assign it [to us] when the night has dawned.
Being thus provoked, they said:
While you yourselves remain, you cause the Teacher’s instruction to disappear; if there is any remorse, point it out [to us], as one does regarding bedding and seating by way of seniority;
for those [others] are strong in speech.
The assigner of lodgings, being terrified, made the assignment;
the group of six monks took their lodgings at the end of the row and lay down; by the time the junior monks were being assigned their places, the night had turned to dawn.
The group of six monks, rising very quickly, said:
"Venerable ones, take up your bedding;
let us go."
They were addressed by the monks:
"Venerable sirs, for the sake of a single night you have disturbed the entire community of monks throughout the whole night; oh, would that you would stay right here!
They replied:
"Nanda and Upananda, let us go to Śrāvastī with all our followers," they said, and having said this, they departed.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
Therefore, monks, bedding and seating should not be assigned during the night; if they arrive at night, they should be accommodated according to their acquaintances. (Disciplinary Prescriptions)
A monk from a certain country, who had come to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the shrine,

was unacquainted with the proper alms-round there; rising very early in the morning, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet, and [after greeting] the elder monks, entered Śrāvastī for alms.

As he was wandering for alms, the time arrived; leaning against the base of a wall right there, he began to eat his meal. And Anāthapiṇḍada set out along that same path, intending to pay homage to the caitya.
He saw him and said:
"Noble one, having gone forth into this teaching which is so entirely pleasing, why do you act with such hostility?
He replied:
"Venerable one, what is this clamor?
Do you not see that the time is near?
He replied:
"Why have you not come to my house?
"What is your name?
"Anāthapiṇḍada."
"I have heard in various sūtras that there is a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada; yet I know neither his protector nor his home.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada reflected:
"This monk has come from afar and is ignorant of my character; he certainly does not know me (nor my house)."
"What would be appropriate here at this time? he thought. "I shall have a walkway constructed from Śrāvastī as far as the Jeta Grove. Having understood this, he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Venerable sir, visiting monks who are unskilled in the proper range for alms-round, while wandering for alms, pass the time and perform their meal-eating by leaning against the base of a wall;
because of this practice, those lacking faith will disparage the Noble Ones."
"Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit it, I would have walkways constructed here between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove,
so that whoever has his mealtime at a particular spot may consume his almsfood there.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, householder, I give you permission; have it built.
He then had walkways constructed between Śrāvastī and the Jeta Grove;
whichever monk’s turn it was, he would perform his meal duties there.
Other monks suffered from a lack of drinking water;

however, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had a well constructed there and a cartload of the three pungent substances and the three fruits was placed therein. That water became delicious and excellent, becoming renowned throughout the entire world.
The multitude of people, having heard [the news], arrived;
the monks tried to stop them,
but the residents of Śrāvastī said:
"We, the noble ones, are at your service with all necessary provisions,
yet you are withholding water that is common to the whole world.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"They should not be prevented.
Then a woman asked the monks for drinking water.
The monks did not grant it;
the Blessed One said:
"It should be granted. Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"The female sex is a universal snare, a bond of Māra.
Monks, while offering water, became infatuated with women;
eventually, a certain woman endowed with beauty and youth, looking longingly at a young monk, requested that water from him.
Even he who, being observant toward her and with a mind full of attachment,
gives [the gift] in an unbroken stream even when being restrained;
likewise, she too gazes [upon him].
"She drank water that had turned poisonous; she has passed away. Monks who had little need for it reproached, reviled, and censured him.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said: "If a woman is full of longing for a monk and her mind is bound to him, one must not give [the requisites] to her oneself."
Nor should water be given to a woman in an unbroken stream;
rather, the stream of water should be interrupted at intervals, or she should be told, "Fill your cupped hands and drink," otherwise one commits an offense of transgression.
At that time, those who used to offer the first alms-food at Jeta’s Grove began to give it right there;
the group-of-six monks heard of this and went to stand on the walking-path.
They ask him by whom the foremost alms-food is brought;
if it is milk-rice, they hold out a bowl;
if it is a drink of water-gruel, [they do likewise].
They say:
"The Saṅgha possesses great supernatural power; that Saṅgha is of great majesty."
"Give it to the Saṃgha. In this way, [the distribution of] solid foods, snacks, and so forth should be coordinated.
The monks, being of little concern, criticize, revile, and speak against [this].
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said: "A monk must not participate in the gains belonging to others."
If one attends [the assembly],
one incurs an offense of transgression;
thus it was said by the Blessed One.
"A monk must not participate in the gains belonging to others.
Now, some monks were going to another monastery on some business;
when they had arrived there, the time for the meal was approaching.
Out of remorse, they did not eat;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and on this occasion the Blessed One said:
"One should not go intentionally; otherwise, if the time for eating has already passed for those who have gone, they should eat, and no remorse should be felt in this matter.
A time of hardship is currently prevailing."
The monks went to another monastery;
seeing the monks there eating, they desired to eat again [out of remorse].
They did not consume it;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said:

If that which was not previously taken in the former monastery is distributed in an unlimited amount, it may be accepted; however, if the number of monks has been fixed, it must not be accepted. If one accepts it [in such a case], one incurs an offense of transgression (sātisāra).
The wicked deeds of the monks Aśvaka and Punarvasuka:
Now at that time, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour through the Kāśī countries, he arrived at Kiṭāgiri.
At that time, two monks named Aśvaka and Punarvasuka were residing at Kiṭāgiri.
They heard:
"The Blessed One, having wandered on a tour through the country of Kāśī, will come here together with the community of monks."
And having heard this, they reflected:
"The monks will challenge us (or remind us) in the presence of the Teacher."
"Or by one who is shameless, or by a ferryman;
what if we, for the sake of the Blessed One, having established a large monastery, were to appoint three assigners of lodgings and six receivers of lodgings among the monks?"
What are the three assigners of lodgings?
The winter, the summer, and the rainy season [assigners].
What are the six receivers of lodgings?
The entire monastery must be assigned;
the entire vicinity of the monastery; and the entire enclosure.
The entire vicinity of the monastery compound,
the entire grove, and the entire vicinity of the grove;
if they say, "Assign the monastery," one should say, "This has already been assigned."
"Point out a courtyard; this one has been pointed out. Point out the vicinity of the monastery; this too has been pointed out. Point out a grove; this too has been pointed out."
"Appoint the vicinity of the grove; this too is appointed.
They were without a dwelling and without a fixed residence, thinking, "They will not reproach us or remind us, whether out of shamelessness or because they are mere intermediaries.
Those two had three assigners of lodgings appointed for them.
There were six recipients of lodgings and seats;
meanwhile, the Blessed One arrived at Kiṭāgiri,
and the two of them had already prepared a monastery for the Blessed One.
The monks said: "Venerable ones, designate a lodging and a dwelling. They replied:
The monastery has been assigned as previously indicated;
assign the cells;
that too has been assigned.
The monastery is the ground surrounding the monastery;
designate the enclosure;
that too has been designated.
"Designate the vicinity of the monastery";
it was designated;
"Designate the vicinity of the enclosure."
That too was designated;
designate a grove;
that too was designated.
"Designate the vicinity of the grove";
that too was designated.
Since they did not designate it in its entirety, a loud noise and a great clamor arose at the edge of the grove.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers who inquire;
they do not inquire out of ignorance.
They inquire at the proper time.
They do not ask what is past its time;
they ask what is connected with the goal; they do not ask what is disconnected from the goal.
The suspension of the bridge occurs when the questions of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are not connected with the goal;
therein, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are knowers of the proper time regarding questions connected with the goal.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, asks the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, why has this loud noise, this great clamor, and the roar of a vast multitude arisen at the edge of the park?
He replied:
"By Aśvaka and Punarvasuka..."
With reference to two monks,
three assigners of lodgings were appointed for the monks,
and six receivers of lodgings.
The monks do not obtain bedding and seats;
because of that, there is this loud noise and great clamor at the edge of the monastery, and the roar of a great multitude of people.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, it was with reference to monks who create strife that I established three assigners of lodgings and six receivers of lodgings;
this does not apply to those who are of natural disposition."

Therefore, monks should not appoint three assigners of lodgings and six receivers of lodgings with reference to monks who are in their natural state; if they do so, they commit an offense. (The mischief of the Six Monks again)
While the Blessed One was wandering on tour through the Kośala country, he arrived at night for a stay in a forest hermitage near a certain small village, together with the community of monks.
The group of six monks, having set aside one beautiful tree for the sake of the Blessed One, took other beautiful trees for themselves.
Hollow trees became the dwellings of the elder monks;
King Prasenajit of Kośala heard of this and went out to meet them with his fourfold army.
Having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, he searched for the elder monks;
eventually he saw the group-of-six monks stationed beneath beautiful trees,
while the elder monks were under hollow trees.
Having said "Hum," he approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, King Prasenajit of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I am a consecrated Kṣatriya king, the lord of all treasures produced within my realm;
every excellent thing belongs to me."
The remainder was distributed as was appropriate among the queens, the princes, the ministers, and the army officers; the Blessed One,
the Supreme King of Dharma,
along with the great śrāvakas such as the noble Kauṇḍinya, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, and Pārāvaṭa, remained stationed at the Koṭa trees.
But the group of six monks [thought] regarding the beautiful trees:
"Oh, would that the Blessed One, out of compassion, were to designate the trees as well according to seniority!
The Blessed One consented to King Prasenajit of Kosala by remaining silent.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala, perceiving through his silence that the Blessed One had consented, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed.
Regarding this occurrence, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, even trees, sacrificial altars, and grassy plots should be assigned according to seniority."
The Blessed One said:
"Even trees and grassy plots should be assigned according to seniority.
Yet the monks were assigning them themselves.
The Blessed One said:
"A monk who assigns dwellings should be appointed.
The monks appointed one without making distinctions.
The Blessed One said:
"Endowed with five qualities, a monk who assigns lodgings, even if not yet appointed, should not be appointed; and if already appointed, he should be dismissed."
By which five?
He acts out of desire, he acts out of hatred, he acts out of delusion, he acts out of fear, and he does not know the designated and non-designated dwelling.
One who is endowed with these five qualities, though unappointed as the assigner of dwellings, should not be appointed.
And one who has been appointed should be dismissed; however, one who possesses five qualities, though not yet appointed as the assigner of dwellings, should be appointed, and once appointed,
should not be dismissed.
By which five?
He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion; and he knows both what has been assigned and what has not been assigned.
Endowed with these five qualities, one who assigns dwellings should be appointed even if not yet appointed.
Once he has been approved, he must not be dismissed. Furthermore, he should be approved in this manner:

having prepared the seating and bedding, having struck the ghaṇṭā, and having exhorted the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha is seated and assembled, [the procedure] should be announced as before. (He...)
If he is able, he should say, "I am able";
after that—
One monk, having made the formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This monk named so-and-so, the assigner of dwellings, is capable of assigning dwellings for the Saṃgha."
If it seems appropriate to the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha should permit it, let the Saṃgha authorize such-and-such a person as the assigner of dwellings; this is the motion (*jñapti*);
the formal act (*karman*) is now to be performed.
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!

This monk named so-and-so, the assigner of dwellings, is capable of assigning dwellings for the Saṃgha. Therefore, the Saṃgha appoints this monk named so-and-so as the assigner of dwellings. Those venerable ones who consent to appointing this monk named so-and-so as the assigner of dwellings should remain silent; those who do not consent..."
Let them speak; the Saṃgha has approved the monk named so-and-so as the assigner of dwellings;
it is accepted and authorized by the Saṃgha since there is silence;
thus do I understand this.
Just as the assigner of lodgings [is appointed], so too are the assigner of meals, the server of rice-gruel, the distributor of hard foods, the distributor of whatever [other food] there may be,
the keeper of utensils, the keeper of robes,
and the distributor of robes.
The guardian of the rainy-season robe, the distributor of the rainy-season robe, and the messenger;
a monk endowed with five qualities who has not been appointed as the overseer of the monastery (*prāsādavārika*) should not be appointed,
and one who has been appointed should be dismissed.
By which five? He goes out of desire, he goes out of hatred, he goes out of delusion, he goes out of fear, and he does not know who is graceful and who is ungraceful.
A monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the superintendent of the monastery hall (*prāsādavārika*), and once appointed, he should not be dismissed. What are these five?
He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear; he discerns what is pleasing and what is unpleasing.
Summary verse:
The distributor of monastery meals, the distributor of rice-gruel and solid food,
the guardian of whatever goods there may be, and the keeper of the two robes.
The one who uses the rainy-season robe, the cowherd, the distributor, the messenger, and likewise the supervisor of the monastery—
these are remembered as the twelve individuals.
The section on bedding and seating is completed.
